name: The Yamamoto Monkeypod

location.address: 5330 Koloa Road, Koloa, HI 96756 (behind the former Yamamoto Store site, Waikomo Stream side)

access: Free, standing in the open courtyard/streetside area of Old Koloa Town behind the historic Yamamoto Store building
transport: In Old Koloa Town, walkable from anywhere on Koloa Road
verify_notes: Register: Hawaii Exceptional Trees (data.honolulu.gov, CC0), register_id 1149, 'In Koloa behind old Yamamoto Store next to river', girth_cm 691.9, vitality Good. Second source oldkoloa.com (the Yamamoto Store's own history page, fetched directly): 'Howard Yamamoto planted the Monkeypod Tree on the Waikomo Stream side, previously named Koloa Stream', during the early 1920s when the Yamamoto family took over the general store (built 1898, rebuilt 1983). That gives a documented planting date for THIS specimen, about 100-105 years by 2026, which is the basis for the age estimate. DISAGREEMENT: fotospot.com (a tourist-photo directory, lower confidence) independently gives the same tree's coordinates (21.903779, -159.46596) and a photo dated 2026-01-02 confirming it is alive and standing now, but claims the tree is 'approximately 130 years old' and links it to the Hitachi logo. That Hitachi-logo tree is well documented elsewhere as a different Monkeypod at Moanalua Gardens on Oahu, so this looks like a mix-up with that tree and is NOT used; the writer should not repeat the Hitachi claim. Flagged for the age conflict (100-105 years from the store's own history vs 130 years from the tourist site) rather than picking a winner silently.

name: The Koloa Baobab

location.address: Koloa Missionary Church, 3370 Poipu Road, Koloa, HI 96756 (behind the church yard, near the southeast corner)

verified_sources: Hawaii Exceptional Trees register (data.honolulu.gov, CC0), register_id 1121
access: Free, in the church yard; a baobab is unmistakable and visible from the grounds
transport: In Old Koloa Town on Poipu Road, walkable from the rest of the cluster
verify_notes: Register: Hawaii Exceptional Trees, register_id 1121, species_latin 'Adasonia sp.' (sic, Adansonia), vitality Excellent, no assessed date, no girth recorded. Locality text: 'Behind the Koloa Missionary Church yard near the southeast corner; TMK: 2-8-10-1'. Second, independent source: The Outdoor Circle's 'My Favorite Tree' entries, 'Baobab - Koloa, Kauai', posted 2016-12-05, confirms existence, species and general location, but carries no age, girth or condition detail. No age basis exists anywhere (no girth to derive from, no planting record found): age_estimate left empty per the estimate-or-ask rule, the page should ask the reader. Flagged because the most recent independent confirmation found is 2016 (10 years old); could not find a 2020s photo or observation specifically of THIS baobab (an iNaturalist search for Adansonia within 5km turned up two 2024/2025 African baobab observations, but they sit ~3km west near Kalaheo/Lawai, not at this church, and are almost certainly a different specimen, likely at the National Tropical Botanical Garden collection; not used as evidence for this tree). Coordinates are the register's 1.1km grid point, not tree-level: pin the church's street address and mark approximate. Baobabs are extremely rare and distinctive in Hawaii, which is itself a reason to trust the register's designation, but that does not substitute for a recent sighting.

name: The Kanoa Banyan Tree

location.address: Niumalu, along Hulemanu Road on the way to the Menehune (Alekoko) Fishpond, approximately 84 feet east of Hulemanu Road

verified_sources: Hawaii Exceptional Trees register (data.honolulu.gov, CC0), register_id 1142
access: Free, visible from the public road to the Menehune Fishpond overlook
transport: Niumalu, about 10-15 min drive/short bike from Lihue town centre
verify_notes: Register: Hawaii Exceptional Trees, register_id 1142, girth_cm 1987.3 (the largest girth of any Kauai entry in the register), height 64 ft, vitality Excellent, locality 'Approximately 84 feet east of Hulemanu Road in Niumalu... on the western boundary of TMK 3-2-02:26'. Second, independent source: The Garden Island newspaper (Kauai's local paper), 2026-08-22 feature 'Island History: the historic banyan trees at Niumalu and Nawiliwili, Kauai', fetched directly: names it the Kanoa Banyan Tree, says it was planted by the men of Paul P. Kanoa, governor of Kauai 1882-1886, in his honor, on what was then Kanoa's property (later the Achi family's), 'still flourishes in Niumalu', and was declared an exceptional tree by Kauai County in 1990 at the Achi family's request. That gives a documented planting window for THIS specimen (1882-1886), which is the basis for the age estimate (about 140 years by 2026), and the newspaper feature is itself alive-now evidence from this month. No conflict between sources; register girth confirms this is a genuinely massive specimen, consistent with a 140-year-old banyan. Coordinates are the register's 1.1km grid point plus Niumalu's hamlet centre from OSM/Nominatim, not a verified tree-level pin, so precision stays approximate despite the strong textual locator (84 feet east of Hulemanu Road).

name: The Wilcox Banyan Tree

location.address: Banyan Harbor Resort, 3411 Wilcox Road, Lihue (Nawiliwili), HI 96766, on the former Papalinahoa Road descending from Kuhiau Ridge

verified_sources: Hawaii Exceptional Trees register (data.honolulu.gov, CC0), register_id 1145
access: Free. The tree stands on the grounds of Banyan Harbor Resort at Nawiliwili, a working condo resort rather than a park. The drive in is open and the tree is visible from it; be aware you are on residential resort ground, not public parkland.
transport: Nawiliwili, a few minutes from Lihue town centre
verify_notes: Register: Hawaii Exceptional Trees, register_id 1145, species_latin Ficus microcarpa (Chinese Banyan), girth_cm 658.4, height 38 ft, vitality Good, locality 'At Nawiliwili north of Highway 501 on the hillside south of Kauai High School, at Menehune Gardens'. Two independent Garden Island (Kauai's local newspaper) features, 2013-01-20 and 2026-08-22, both fetched directly, name it the Wilcox Banyan Tree: planted in 1895 by George N. Wilcox (Grove Farm Co. owner) on a curve of the old Papalinahoa Road, now standing on Banyan Harbor Resort property at Nawiliwili, covering about two acres with 1,000+ air roots, height about 110 feet (the register's 38 ft figure is presumably canopy/crown height at last assessment and is much lower, or measures a different dimension; recorded as-is, flagged as a size disagreement for the writer). Declared an exceptional tree by Kauai County in 1976 after cultural guardian Sarah Kailikea's advocacy; the 2026 article confirms it 'still flourishes' as of this year. Documented planting date (1895) gives the age estimate, about 130 years by 2026. Register locality text (Menehune Gardens, hillside south of Kauai High School) differs somewhat from the newspaper's own description (Banyan Harbor Resort, former Papalinahoa Road) but both place it at Nawiliwili and the species and history line up exactly; treated as the same tree. Access note: it stands on resort grounds, appears to be a public/guest area rather than gated private housing based on Yelp/resort site descriptions, but a visitor should expect it is a functioning condo resort rather than a park.

name: The Tree Tunnel (Maluhia Road)

location.address: Maluhia Road, from Knudsen Gap northward for about 3/4 mile toward Koloa, Kauai

verified_sources: Hawaii Exceptional Trees register (data.honolulu.gov, CC0), register_id 1138
access: Free, a public road; drive or walk under the canopy (there is a narrow shoulder, most people experience it from a car or bike)
transport: On Maluhia Road (Hwy 520), the gateway between Lihue/Kaumualii Highway and Koloa/Poipu; no public transit stop, a car or bike is the practical way to reach it
verify_notes: Register: Hawaii Exceptional Trees, register_id 1138, species_latin Eucalyptus robusta (Swamp Mahogany), vitality Excellent, locality 'Along both sides of Maluhia Road extending 3/4 of a mile southward from Knudsen Gap'. Independent sources (Aloha State Daily, 2025-07-23, fetched directly; multiple Kauai tourism sites) confirm this is the famous 'Tree Tunnel', over 500 eucalyptus trees along nearly a mile of Maluhia Road, recognized by Kauai County as an exceptional/historical resource since 1976. PLANTING DATE DISAGREEMENT, recorded rather than resolved: most sources credit pineapple/sugar figure Walter Duncan McBryde with planting the trees around 1911 from leftover nursery stock at his Kukuiolono estate; one source (Aloha State Daily) also records a competing local account crediting the Knudsen family with planting them to stabilize a marshy lane and act as a windbreak. Age estimate (roughly 115 years, ~100-130) is based on the more widely repeated 1911 date. ALIVE NOW: strongly confirmed, the 2025 article describes the canopy as 'green and full' and documents its recovery after Hurricane Iniki (1992) stripped the canopy to bare branches; residents said it would grow back and it did within a few years. TREATED AS ONE ENSEMBLE ENTRY, not as individual trees, per the collectible-point rule: it is famous specifically as a single unified landmark (a tunnel/gateway) rather than as any individual tree, and there is one obvious place to experience it, driving or standing at the entrance near Koloa. Pin is an OpenStreetMap tourism=attraction node literally named 'Tree Tunnel' on Maluhia Road; still approximate because it marks a representative point along a near-mile-long feature, not a single trunk. Girth not applicable to an ensemble of hundreds of trees, left empty.

name: The Gulick-Rowell Monkeypod

location.address: Gulick-Rowell House, 9567 Huakai Road, Waimea, HI 96796

verified_sources: Hawaii Exceptional Trees register (data.honolulu.gov, CC0), register_id 1148
access: Free, from the street. The monkeypod stands in the front yard of the Gulick-Rowell House on Huakai Road, a historic house under restoration and not open to visitors. The tree fills the yard and is in full view from the public road; the pin marks where to stand.
transport: In Waimea town, walkable from the town centre
verify_notes: Register: Hawaii Exceptional Trees, register_id 1148, girth_cm 853.4 (the largest monkeypod girth of any Kauai entry), height 68 ft, vitality Excellent, locality 'In Waimea in front of the historical Gulick-Towell home' (register spells it Gulick-Towell, the house's actual and correct name is Gulick-Rowell, NRHP #78001027, built by Rev. Peter Johnson Gulick from 1829, completed by Rev. George Rowell by 1846). Second, independent source: bigislandnow.com, 2024-04-08, fetched directly, on the Hale Puna restoration project: 'the site is readily identified by the gargantuan monkeypod shading its front yard; tradition claims it is the first such tree planted on the Garden Isle... tradition claims the Gulick-Rowell House's monkeypod tree is 200 years old, and a gift to Hawai'i from an Indian prince', and confirms it is STILL STANDING as of 2024 ('the monkeypod tree remains standing... providing shade'; wood from a pruned portion has been repurposed into tables at Kokee Lodge, which implies active tree management rather than removal). A third source (kauai.com blog, fetched directly) independently confirms the tree still stands today. AGE: the '200 years, gift from an Indian prince' claim is explicitly local TRADITION, not a documented record, and it does not survive a sanity check: other sources place the introduction of monkeypod (Albizia/Samanea saman) to Hawaii at 1847 (Peter A. Brinsmade, Oahu), which is only about 179 years before 2026, so a 200-year-old specimen predates the species' known arrival by roughly two decades. Recorded as a folklore claim worth mentioning in the story AS folklore, but NOT used as our age_estimate, which is left empty for the page to ask the reader; girth (853.4cm, the largest of the cluster) is recorded and could support a derived estimate once a published Albizia saman growth rate is sourced. Location is confirmed at the house's own street address (9567 Huakai Road), geocoded via OpenStreetMap/Nominatim; the tree itself stands in the identifiable front yard of a single well-documented historic house, not a broad area.
